accuracy.evidence: Splits coping the way the research does: problem-focused coping changes the situation and emotion-focused coping changes the feeling when it cannot be changed (Lazarus and Folkman 1984; Compas et al. 2017 meta-analysis of child coping). Anger is framed as high arousal that needs lowering first and sadness as low energy that responds to comfort and connection, worded as 'best fit first' rather than 'only works for', so no tool is called useless.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the slips teachers see at 7 to 9: one favourite tool for every feeling (step 1 prediction), a home tool at school such as going to the bedroom (step 2 prediction and spot feedback), trying hard to fix the unfixable like rain (step 3 prediction), giving up when the first tool half works (step 4 prediction), and talking a fight through while still boiling.

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanics are about choosing between strategies, not doing one: a one-card-at-a-time deal into an anger jar and a sadness jar, a school/home switch that changes which tools are allowed, a fixable/unfixable sort, a sad meter that only drops a little for a poor-fit tool, and a feeling-then-tool plan builder. It shares no mechanic with flagcalm's balloon and stepping stones or flagcool's decision tree, and passed the 30% shingle gate.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner finds the rule by doing: the sadness jar refuses the stress ball with a reason, the bedroom tile turns red at school but works after switching to home, rain cannot go in the fix jar, and Sam's meter starts at 4 after breaths so the learner sees a half-working tool and then a fitting one take it to 1. The plan step makes them name the feeling before any tool is offered.

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab then disproves: one tool fits all, go to the bedroom at school, Leo can fix the rain if he tries, and give up because nothing works. The task-done message restates whether the learner's prediction was right and why.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge questions with eleven distinct m= messages that name the slip: arguing while boiling, napping to cool anger, a stress ball for sadness, trying to change the unchangeable, a home tool in class, giving up, the same tool louder, staying cross all day, one tool for everything, and only grown-ups needing tools.

readability.evidence: Kid text measured FK 0.9 against the family limit of 5.0, built on concrete images (toolbox, a spoon cannot fix a bike, hot face, tight fists, curling up). Adult text measured FK 10.0 against the 10.0 limit and names the two coping families in plain terms. Canvas labels are two to five words and wrap inside their tiles.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler regex and the 12% duplication gate against all 242 earlier lessons. Each kid paragraph teaches one idea (no single tool, anger tools, sadness tools, place and fixability), and the family tip gives one concrete artefact: a school/home by angry/sad/worried coping card reviewed after the next upset.

mobile.evidence: Checked on 360x640 Android light and iPhone 13 dark screenshots of every step: the young class gives large buttons, the two jars and the dealt card fit side by side at 360 px, the six place tiles drop to two columns on narrow screens, tool tiles wrap 'Video call his friend' to two lines, and every canvas target also has a button below.

accessibility.evidence: axe-core WCAG 2.1 AA clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone in the walkthrough, with no console errors. Every drag (card to jar, tool to Sam) and every tap target has a labelled button, the canvas aria-label reads the current card, place, meter level and story, and right or wrong is shown by text as well as colour.
